question: Between which latitudes is the North Atlantic airspace most heavily used?
explanation: The airspace over the North Atlantic between about 35°N and 70°N is among the busiest oceanic airspace in the world.

question: What name is now used for the North Atlantic airspace with special navigation requirements, formerly MNPS airspace?
explanation: The airspace formerly called minimum navigation performance specification (MNPS) airspace is now called NAT high level airspace (HLA). Its vertical limits and approval requirement continue.

question: Why does North Atlantic traffic tend to concentrate at the same levels?

options.text: Higher levels are reserved for the military
Lower levels are always in icing conditions
Jets are most efficient near the tropopause

explanation: Turbine aeroplanes are most efficient where the air is coldest yet thin, around the tropopause, so most traffic wants to cruise at or near it.

question: At about what latitudes do the polar front and subtropical jet streams lie over the North Atlantic?
explanation: The polar front jet lies at about 55°N and the subtropical jet at about 40°N over the North Atlantic, both flowing west to east.

question: About how high is the tropopause at 40°N compared with 55°N over the North Atlantic?

options.text: About 40 000 ft at 40°N and 35 000 ft at 55°N
About 45 000 ft at 40°N and 25 000 ft at 55°N
About 35 000 ft at 40°N and 40 000 ft at 55°N

explanation: The tropopause is higher nearer the equator: about 40 000 ft at 40°N and about 35 000 ft at 55°N.

question: Which of these is a navigation problem over the North Atlantic?

options.text: No ground-based radio navigation aids in mid-ocean
Strong magnetic fields over the sea that upset the compasses

explanation: Transoceanic problems include no aerodromes, no ground radar, no fixed radio aids and reliance on HF beyond VHF range.

question: Why are radio aids at very high northern latitudes aligned with true north?

options.text: True north is easier to print on charts
Aircraft compasses only show true north
Weak horizontal field and large variation

explanation: North of about 70°N the horizontal component of the earth's field is weak and variation can be large, so beacons are aligned to true north and grid navigation with gyro compasses is used.

question: Under which flight rules must all traffic fly across the North Atlantic at high level?
explanation: Traffic density, separation and navigation requirements mean all traffic crossing the North Atlantic must fly IFR.

question: Between which levels is the North Atlantic oceanic airspace Class A?
explanation: The North Atlantic oceanic airspace is Class A between FL55 and FL660, forming oceanic control areas.

question: What are the vertical limits of NAT high level airspace?
explanation: NAT HLA (formerly MNPS airspace) extends from FL285 to FL420, incorporating the RVSM levels FL290 to FL410.

question: How many oceanic control areas make up the North Atlantic high level airspace?
explanation: There are five OCAs: Shanwick, Santa Maria, Gander, New York and Reykjavik.

question: From which location is the Shanwick oceanic area controlled?
explanation: The OACCs are Prestwick (Shanwick), Lisbon (Santa Maria), Gander, New York and Reykjavik.

question: Along which meridian is the boundary between Shanwick and Gander?
explanation: The east-west boundary is at 30°W between Shanwick and Gander, and at 40°W between Santa Maria and New York.

question: Along which parallel is the boundary between Shanwick/Gander and Santa Maria/New York?
explanation: The north-south boundary between those pairs of OCAs is at 45°N.

question: Which oceanic area extends to the North Pole and covers most of Greenland?
explanation: Reykjavik OCA extends from the northern boundaries of Shanwick and Gander to the North Pole, including most of Greenland.

question: What is the West Atlantic Route System (WATRS)?

options.text: A track system across the Arctic
USA–Caribbean routes south-west of the HLA
The transition area west of Ireland
The routes for aircraft with one long-range navigation system

explanation: Beyond the south-west boundary of the NAT HLA, New York oceanic airspace contains the WATRS routes between the USA and the Caribbean.

subtopic: Approval and the Mach number technique
question: What must an operator have before flying in NAT high level airspace?

options.text: Only a letter from the oceanic centre

explanation: Operators need authority approval, shown on the AOC, for the aircraft to navigate to the required performance in the NAT HLA.

subtopic: Approval and the Mach number technique
question: Why do aircraft on the same track at the same level fly the same Mach number?

options.text: It is the speed shown on the track message
It uses less fuel than any other speed
It allows them to overtake safely
They keep a near-constant time interval

explanation: Aircraft flying the same Mach number on the same route and level experience similar wind and temperature, so time intervals between them remain nearly constant.

subtopic: Approval and the Mach number technique
question: Which Mach number is entered in the flight plan for a NAT crossing?

options.text: The indicated Mach number with no correction
The Mach number used by the aircraft ahead

explanation: The requested true Mach number, taking account of known errors in the flight deck indication, is entered in the flight plan.

subtopic: Approval and the Mach number technique
question: By how much may ATC change the requested Mach number?
explanation: ATC may occasionally assign a Mach number 0.01 higher than, or 0.02 lower than, the requested one.

subtopic: Approval and the Mach number technique
question: During a step climb in oceanic airspace, what Mach number should be flown?

options.text: Any Mach number, until level again
The Mach number for the new level

explanation: Pilots should keep their last assigned Mach number during step climbs; if performance does not allow, they must tell ATC when requesting the climb.

subtopic: Approval and the Mach number technique
question: After leaving oceanic airspace, what Mach number must the aircraft fly?

options.text: The assigned one, until domestic ATC changes it
Any Mach number the crew choose
The best-range Mach number at once

explanation: After leaving oceanic airspace, pilots must keep the assigned Mach number in domestic airspace until the ATC unit authorises a change.

question: Within NAT HLA, which RVSM levels are included?
explanation: The NAT HLA extends from FL285 to FL420, incorporating the RVSM levels FL290 to FL410.

question: During the times of the organised track system, which levels may be used in each direction on the tracks?
explanation: Because of the tidal flow, during OTS periods all levels are available in the direction of the tracks; outside the OTS standard RVSM levels apply.

question: What is the maximum difference allowed between the two primary altimeters for RVSM?
explanation: RVSM requires two independent altimeters agreeing within ±200 ft, an autopilot height hold, an altitude deviation alert (at least aural at ±300 ft) and a Mode C transponder.

question: What must a crew do if the aircraft deviates by more than 300 ft from its cleared level in RVSM airspace?

options.text: Squawk 7700 until back at the level
Only note it in the technical log
Nothing, if the level is regained
Report it to ATS, then in writing

explanation: A height deviation of more than 300 ft must be reported to ATS, with a written report after the flight.

question: What is the minimum long-range navigation equipment for NAT HLA?

options.text: One long-range navigation system plus VOR/DME as a backup

explanation: The minimum is two independent long-range navigation systems (GNSS, INS or IRS), each giving continuous position, track and speed.

question: Which of these is an approved long-range navigation system?
explanation: Approved long-range navigation systems include GNSS, INS and IRS.

question: An aircraft has three long-range navigation systems and one fails before entry. May it continue as planned?

options.text: No, it must leave the HLA
Only on a Blue Spruce route

explanation: With triple systems, one unserviceable still leaves the required two, so the flight can proceed as planned.

question: Which ACAS requirement applies to large turbine aeroplanes in the North Atlantic region?

options.text: ACAS II for large turbine aeroplanes
No ACAS, because there is no radar

explanation: All turbine aeroplanes over 5700 kg or with more than 19 passenger seats must carry and operate ACAS II in the NAT region.

question: Why is an organised track system (OTS) set up across the North Atlantic?

options.text: To separate military and civil traffic
To route traffic around the jet streams
To handle the tidal flow on similar routes
To keep aircraft over land as long as possible

explanation: Traffic follows similar minimum time tracks at similar times in each direction, so roughly parallel, effectively one-way tracks are set up for each flow.

question: Is the use of the organised tracks mandatory?

options.text: No; random routes may be planned

explanation: Using the OTS is not mandatory. A route not following the OTS is a random route, subject to restrictions to protect OTS traffic.

question: How are the daytime (westbound) tracks lettered?

options.text: From A, the most southerly, northwards
By number, from 1 in the north
From A, the most northerly, southwards
From Z, the most southerly, northwards

explanation: Daytime westbound tracks are lettered from A for the most northerly at the start point, sequentially southwards.

question: How are the night-time (eastbound) tracks lettered?

options.text: From Z, the most southerly, then Y, X northwards
From A, the most northerly, southwards
By number, from 1 in the south
From Z, the most northerly, then southwards in reverse order

explanation: Night-time eastbound tracks start with Z for the most southerly, then Y and so on northwards.

question: Where is the period of validity of the OTS defined?
explanation: The OTS period is defined at 30°W, roughly mid-ocean; to fly a track, an aircraft must plan to cross 30°W within the OTS period.

question: What is the usual validity of the daytime westbound OTS at 30°W?
explanation: The standard periods are 1130–1900 UTC at 30°W for the westbound OTS and 0100–0800 UTC for the eastbound OTS.

question: What is the usual validity of the night-time eastbound OTS at 30°W?
explanation: The eastbound OTS is normally valid from 0100 to 0800 UTC at 30°W.

question: What is the purpose of the changeover periods between the two OTS?

options.text: To let military aircraft cross the ocean
So one OTS empties before the reverse one opens
To allow controllers a meal break
To give time for the track message to be printed

explanation: A changeover (buffer) period between the end of one OTS and the start of the reverse one lets an aircraft crossing 30°W at the end of an OTS complete the route safely.

question: Which oceanic centre publishes the daytime westbound OTS?
explanation: Shanwick publishes the daytime (westbound) OTS and Gander the night-time (eastbound) OTS.

question: How can an operator ask for a particular route to be considered when the OTS is planned?

options.text: By telephoning the oceanic controller on the day
By requesting it on the first HF position report
By sending a preferred route message in advance

explanation: Operators can request routings by submitting a preferred route message (PRM) before the planning conference.

question: What does a track message identifier (TMI) consist of?

options.text: The flight number of the first aircraft on the track
The OACC name, "TMI" and the Julian date of the OTS
The track letter and the entry point

explanation: The TMI is the name of the OACC, the abbreviation TMI and the Julian date (day of the year) of the OTS.

question: What is the Julian date for 28 February?
explanation: January has 31 days, so 28 February is day 31 + 28 = 59, written 059.

question: The OTS for 15 March in a non-leap year has which Julian date?
explanation: 31 (January) + 28 (February) + 15 = 74, written 074. In a leap year it would be 075.

question: How is an amendment to the NAT track message shown?

options.text: It is reissued in full with a suffix letter, e.g. 059A
A new Julian date is used
Only the changed track is sent
The amended track is given a number instead of a letter

explanation: If an amendment is needed, the whole track message is reissued and the TMI gets a suffix letter, such as TMI 059A, then B.

question: In a track message, what does the position "59/10" mean?
explanation: The 5-character group gives whole degrees of latitude, a slash, then whole degrees of longitude west: 59/10 means 5900N 01000W.

question: In a track message, what does "EAST LVLS NIL" indicate for a westbound track?

options.text: Eastbound traffic may use any level
The track is closed for the day
No eastbound levels on that track
No levels are available east of 30°W

explanation: EAST LVLS NIL means no levels are allocated to opposite-direction traffic on that track during the OTS period.

question: Which levels on the tracks are often not allocated in the track message?
explanation: FL290 and 300 are usually too low and FL400 and 410 rather high for normal traffic, and leaving them out frees levels for non-OTS traffic.

question: What part of the track message gives the routing from the exit point into North American airspace?
explanation: The NAR entries give the North American routes from the exit point; EUR RTS WEST gives European routes to the entry point.

question: What should be included in the read-back of an oceanic clearance on an organised track?

options.text: The whole route in full, every time
The track letter and the TMI number

explanation: An abbreviated read-back is allowed, replacing the route details with the track letter plus the TMI; without them, the full route must be read back.

question: What proportion of gross navigation errors occur after a reroute, according to track message remarks?
explanation: Track message remarks warn that about 80% of gross navigation errors occur after a reroute, so waypoint cross-checks must always be done.

question: Which of these would be a random route?

options.text: Any route on the published OTS, flown at a non-OTS level
Track A flown during its period
Track Z flown during its period
A route that crosses 30°W outside the OTS period

explanation: Random routes include the reciprocal of an OTS track, part of a track, a route crossing 30°W outside the OTS period, one completely outside the OTS, or one crossing tracks.

question: An operator plans a random route using part of the OTS. Which tracks should it use?

options.text: Any track with the most levels
The track with the fewest aircraft

explanation: If part of the OTS is used, the outer (most northerly or most southerly) tracks should be planned for that part.

question: What is the polar track structure (PTS) today?

options.text: The main route system north of 70°N
A system of routes for helicopters

explanation: The polar track structure no longer exists.

question: What are Blue Spruce routes?

options.text: Routes for aircraft with one long-range system
Routes reserved for twin-engine ETOPS aircraft

explanation: Blue Spruce routes are special routes for aircraft with only one serviceable long-range navigation system; approval for the high level airspace is still needed.

question: What do North American routes (NARs) provide?

options.text: A link between oceanic and North American airspace

explanation: NARs are numbered predetermined routes linking NAT oceanic airspace and North American domestic airspace, republished on a 56-day cycle.

question: What is NERS?

options.text: A navigation system for one-LRNS aircraft
A European link for eastbound traffic leaving the NAT

explanation: The North Atlantic European Routing Scheme links eastbound traffic leaving the NAT to major European airports; it is published only when traffic warrants.

question: Who provides air traffic service in the Shannon Oceanic Transition Area (SOTA)?

options.text: Shannon ACC, call sign SHANNON CONTROL

explanation: SOTA and NOTA are parts of the Shanwick OCA where Shannon ACC provides the service as SHANNON CONTROL. BOTA is served by Brest Control.

question: What are oceanic transition areas such as SOTA and BOTA used for?

options.text: Holding aircraft before the ocean crossing
Level changes between OTS and domestic levels

explanation: Because the OTS uses all levels one way, transition areas allow level changes as aircraft join or leave domestic routes without loss of separation.

question: What is the primary method of voice communication across the North Atlantic?
explanation: Because of the distances, HF SSB voice has been the primary method, with long-range VHF within about 250 NM of land and datalink increasingly used.

question: Within about what distance of land is long-range VHF available over the North Atlantic?
explanation: Long-range VHF is available within about 250 NM of land, which also allows oceanic clearances to be given by VHF.

question: What is the VHF air-to-air frequency in the North Atlantic?
explanation: 123.45 MHz is the VHF air-to-air frequency, used for example to talk to another aircraft about communication or navigation problems.

question: Which two VHF frequencies must aircraft monitor in the NAT high level airspace?
explanation: All aircraft must monitor 121.5 MHz, and should monitor the air-to-air frequency 123.45 MHz.

question: Who handles routine air-ground voice messages on NAT HF frequencies?

options.text: Radio operators who relay to the controllers

explanation: Routine voice communications go through aeradio stations staffed by communicators with no executive ATC authority, who relay messages to and from the controllers.

question: How does HF frequency choice change between day and night for the same distance?

options.text: A lower frequency is needed by day
The same frequency works at all times

explanation: As a general rule, "the higher the sun, the higher the frequency": a station 1000 NM away needs a higher frequency by day than at night.

question: What does a pilot mean by calling "Shanwick, Skyway 289 on 88"?

options.text: He is 88 NM from the coast

explanation: The ground operator monitors a family of frequencies; "on 88" tells him the aircraft is calling on 8864 kHz.

question: A SATCOM voice call is needed because other means have failed. Whom should it normally be made to?

options.text: The ATC centre directly in all cases
The aeradio station, unless it is urgent

explanation: Since oceanic traffic normally works through aeradio facilities, a SATCOM call should be made to such a facility rather than the ATC centre, unless urgency dictates otherwise.

question: When must the SELCAL check be done for a NAT crossing?

options.text: After landing, for the maintenance log
Only if the HF radio has failed

explanation: The SELCAL code is filed in the flight plan, the system is checked with the aeradio station at or before oceanic entry, and a SELCAL watch is then kept.

question: Must the SELCAL procedure still be followed when CPDLC or SATCOM is used for routine messages?
explanation: The SELCAL provisions must be followed even if datalink or SATCOM is used for routine communication, so ATC can contact the aircraft promptly.

question: What type of air traffic control is used across most of the North Atlantic?

options.text: Procedural control based on position reports
No control at all; only flight information and alerting

explanation: The NAT system has used procedural control, relying on position reports (voice or datalink) to confirm separation.

question: East-west tracks cross whole degrees of latitude at which longitude interval?
explanation: East-west tracks cross each 10° of longitude at whole degrees of latitude, giving reporting points roughly every 500 NM and intervals of about an hour.

question: North of 70°N, at what longitude interval are position reports made?
explanation: Above 70°N position reports are made at intervals of 20° of longitude, because meridians converge.

question: In a NAT voice position report, in what form are times given?
explanation: All times in NAT messages are expressed in hours and minutes UTC, and the message type is stated at the start.

question: A crew using datalink is told "voice position reports not required". What does this mean?

options.text: The crew need not report at all for the whole crossing
The aircraft is under radar control

explanation: Aircraft participating in datalink reporting may be told that voice position reports are not required, because the reports go automatically.

question: After radio failure in the NAT region, what does the pilot maintain?

options.text: The level and speed of the nearest aircraft
The flight-planned level and speed from the moment of failure
A descent to FL285 and the cruise speed
The last acknowledged clearance to the last oceanic point

explanation: The pilot maintains the last received and acknowledged oceanic clearance, including level and speed, to the last specified oceanic route point (normally landfall), then follows the State's procedures.

question: A radio-failed aircraft was cleared on a route other than its flight plan. What does it do after the last oceanic point?

options.text: Land at the first coastal aerodrome
State procedures, then rejoin the filed route
Continue on the oceanic clearance to destination

explanation: After the last oceanic point it conforms to State procedures and rejoins the filed route via the published route structure where possible.

question: How long before reaching the NAT oceanic boundary should an oceanic clearance be requested?
explanation: Pilots should obtain an oceanic clearance at least 40 minutes before entering NAT oceanic airspace. If departing closer than that, the clearance is obtained on the ground.

question: Which three elements make up an oceanic clearance?

options.text: Route, Mach number and flight level

explanation: The three elements are route, Mach number and flight level, providing lateral, longitudinal and vertical separation.

question: After receiving an oceanic clearance, when must a revised entry estimate be passed?

options.text: When it changes by 10 minutes or more
When the estimate changes by 3 minutes or more
Never, once the clearance has been read back correctly
Only if it changes by over 1 minute

explanation: The pilot monitors the forward estimate for oceanic entry and passes a revised estimate if it changes by 3 minutes or more.

question: The oceanic clearance differs from the flight plan. What error must crews especially avoid?

options.text: Requesting a different Mach number after entry
Following the flight plan instead of the clearance

explanation: A significant proportion of NAT navigation errors involve aircraft following the flight plan rather than a differing clearance.

question: The oceanic clearance has a different entry point or level from the current domestic clearance. Who obtains the domestic reclearance?

options.text: The domestic controller, without being asked

explanation: The pilot is responsible for requesting and obtaining the necessary domestic reclearance.

question: What is the strategic lateral offset procedure (SLOP)?

options.text: Offsetting up to 15 NM to either side
Changing level by 500 ft to avoid wake
The centre line or a small offset right of track

explanation: SLOP lets aircraft fly the centre line or an offset of up to 2 NM to the right of track, reducing collision risk and allowing escape from wake turbulence.

question: Under SLOP, to which side may an aircraft offset?
explanation: Strategic lateral offsets are made to the right of the cleared track only, up to 2 NM.

question: Before deviating laterally to avoid severe weather, what should the pilot try to obtain?

options.text: A new oceanic clearance from the next centre only
A revised clearance and traffic information
Nothing; weather deviations need no clearance

explanation: The pilot should request a revised clearance and essential traffic information before deviating, even for small deviations.

question: Without a clearance, which of these should a crew deviating around weather do?

options.text: Broadcast on 121.5 MHz and turn on all lights

explanation: If no clearance can be obtained: deviate away from the track system if possible, broadcast identification, level, position and intentions on 121.5 MHz (or 123.45), watch for traffic visually and by ACAS, and turn on exterior lights.

question: Under the current weather deviation procedure without clearance, when must a level change be made?

options.text: For any deviation, a 1000 ft change at once
Never; the level is always kept
Over 5 NM: change 300 ft at about 5 NM

explanation: Under the current procedure, deviations of less than 5 NM stay at the assigned level; for greater deviations, when about 5 NM from track, a level change of 300 ft is made, direction depending on track and deviation.

question: An aircraft cannot obtain a revised clearance and must leave its track. Under the current contingency procedure, how should it turn?

options.text: At least 45° to the left, to an offset of 15 NM
Exactly 90° to the right, to an offset of 30 NM
Any direction, to an offset of 1 NM
At least 30°, to a 5 NM offset

explanation: The current procedure is to turn at least 30° to the right or left to establish a parallel track offset by 5 NM. Older procedures used a 45° turn and a 15 NM offset.

question: Under the current contingency procedure, what level change follows the 5 NM offset (when able to maintain level)?

options.text: Keep the same level and continue on the offset track
Climb or descend 500 ft to a level not normally used

explanation: Once established on the offset, the aircraft climbs or descends to a level that differs from those normally used by 500 ft.

question: What should an aircraft that cannot maintain its assigned level do first?

options.text: Minimise its descent rate as far as practicable

explanation: An aircraft unable to keep its level should first minimise its rate of descent, then turn while descending to establish the offset track, and select a level differing from normal levels.

question: What determines the direction of the contingency turn, where possible?

options.text: Its position relative to the track system

explanation: The direction is determined, where possible, by the aircraft's position relative to any organised route or track system, and also by alternates, terrain and levels on adjacent tracks.

question: A navigation system fails before entering NAT high level airspace and leaves only one. Which is an acceptable option?

options.text: Continue into the HLA as planned
Enter the HLA and tell ATC later
Fly the track using the magnetic compass only
Stay outside the HLA or use a special route

explanation: Never enter the HLA with unresolved navigation problems. Options include repairing the system, landing, remaining outside the HLA (for example below FL285) or re-filing on a special route for such aircraft.

question: With two systems, one fails after entering NAT high level airspace. How should the flight continue?

options.text: By following the nearest aircraft visually
By leaving the airspace immediately without a clearance
As cleared, consulting the OACC before deviating

explanation: The flight continues in accordance with its clearance; the pilot assesses the situation, prepares a proposal, consults the OACC and obtains a reclearance before deviating.

question: Both long-range navigation systems fail in NAT high level airspace. Which of these should the pilot consider?

options.text: Increasing speed to leave the airspace sooner
A 500 ft level change and all lights on
Flying towards the nearest track centre line

explanation: The pilot should notify the OACC, use information from other aircraft, keep a good lookout, use exterior lights, consider a 500 ft level change and revert to manual navigation.

question: What is an ATC system loop error?

options.text: A failure of the HF radio
An error in the aircraft's altimeter
A wrong waypoint typed into the FMS

explanation: An ATC system loop error is any error caused by a misunderstanding between pilot and controller about the assigned level, Mach number or route.

question: What is a waypoint insertion error?

options.text: Wrong waypoint data in the navigation system

explanation: Many track-keeping errors result from crews programming incorrect waypoint data, often from not checking waypoints against the cleared route or not cross-checking the systems.

question: When cross-checking the route loaded in the FMS, how should the comparison be made?

options.text: From the system to the master document
From the master document to the system
By the dispatcher before departure only

explanation: Ideally each pilot loads the route independently and the other checks it, reading the position in the system and comparing it with the master document, rather than the other way round.

question: Which check must be made before a NAT crossing as well as at each waypoint?
explanation: Before entering oceanic airspace, crews check SELCAL, the master clock and the altimeters (within 200 ft of each other, noting the standby difference); altimeters are compared at each waypoint and disagreements over 200 ft reported.

question: Which time-related check is part of the pre-flight procedure for a NAT crossing?

options.text: A UTC time check and clock reset
Setting the clock to the time of the track message
A check of the local time at destination
A check that the cabin clocks agree

explanation: Pre-flight procedures must include a UTC time check and resynchronisation of the master clock, since position reports and separation depend on accurate times.
